source.title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness
source.authors: U. Macar; Li Yang; Atticus Wang; P. Wallich; E. Ameisen; Jack Lindsey

record.tranche_reason: The study uses refusal-direction ablation, following Arditi et al., to increase detection of injected concepts. It reports introspection outcomes, not whether ablation removes refusal to harmful requests, induces refusal to harmless requests, or preserves general capability as the claim versions require.
record.gate_note: The study computes refusal directions from harmful versus harmless instructions and ablates them, but does not report a harmful-request refusal outcome for that ablation. Its reported ablation results concern detection of injected thoughts, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The ≥30% refusal-bypass criterion in Appendix C.2 is used to select an ablation dose, not reported as an outcome. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study ablates the Arditi-style difference-in-means refusal direction only as a tool to raise injected-thought detection. It reports no refusal rate on harmful or harmless prompts after ablation or addition, and no general-capability check. The harm and coherence judging in Appendix C.1 and the ≥30% refusal-bypass threshold in Appendix C.2 are used only to choose ablation weights. They are not reported as outcomes, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that introspective detection relies on a distributed two-stage circuit (evidence carriers suppressing gates) that emerges from contrastive preference training. They state this circuit is robust to refusal ablation and thus independent of refusal mechanisms. They also conclude refusal ablation unlocks underelicited detection, as refusal-trained denial of internal states suppresses it. They do not test whether the direction mediates refusal of harmful requests.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means refusal directions from harmful versus harmless instructions and projection ablation, following Arditi et al. The study computes a separate direction per layer and, for Gemma3-27B, optimizes weights across 14 layer regions; it uses ablation to elicit introspective detection rather than evaluating refusal behavior.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported introspection effects vary with steering strength and injection layer; cross-model peak gains vary, with the stated endpoints from +14.6% to +58.2%.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the refusal direction in Gemma3-27B raised injected-thought detection from 10.8% to 63.8% and introspection from 4.6% to 24.1%. FPR rose from 0% to 7.3% (α=2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction ablation releases suppressed self-reports of internal states, consistent with the refusal direction also carrying denial of having thoughts.

fits_no_version.finding: Across five 8B–32B models, a minimal-dose refusal-direction ablation raised TPR−FPR, with peak gains from +14.6% to +58.2%. A magnitude-matched random-direction control stayed at or below baseline at most configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of refusal-direction ablation on introspective reporting is direction-specific and generalizes across models.

fits_no_version.finding: The direction separating detected from undetected concepts is nearly orthogonal to the refusal direction (cos = −0.09). The gate-feature circuit and the L45 MLP localization persist in the abliterated model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The anomaly-detection circuit is independent of the refusal direction.

record.problems: For the claim at issue, the study does not report harmful- or harmless-request refusal outcomes after refusal-direction ablation. Its behavioral metrics rely on an LLM judge. Most experiments focus on Gemma3-27B; the cross-model ablation figure has confidence intervals, but the text does not give individual numeric gains for every model.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C.2 reports a sweep in Figure 20; individual values for models other than the stated peak-gain endpoints are not given in the text and were not transcribed from the figure. Dose-selection criteria and values used to select ablation weights are not outcome rows.

untested.parts: No refusal rate on harmful or harmless requests after ablation or addition of the direction, and no capability-preservation measure. Bypass judging is used only to tune ablation weights (App. C.1, C.2).
An abliterated Gemma3-27B is released on HuggingFace, but its refusal rate on harmful prompts is not reported.
Not tested. JailbreakHub results concern the learned bias vector, not the refusal direction.
Not tested for refusal. The multi-direction analysis concerns detection of injected concepts.
Directions are recomputed per model, and no cross-model or cross-language transfer of a direction is tested.
The training-stage comparisons concern introspection, not whether a removable refusal direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly marked as bearing on no version. The Appendix C.1 harm and coherence optimization and the C.2 minimum-dose ≥30% bypass criterion are dose selection, rightly excluded. The reported coherence degradation (“brain damage”) of the abliterated model appears only under strong concept steering, so it does not measure abliteration's capability cost. The small ablation weights (w ≤ 0.3, the smallest reaching 30% bypass) suggest partial ablation, but no refusal outcome is given.

versions.untested_parts: No reported harmful- or harmless-request refusal outcome after direction ablation or addition; no test of preserving general capability under that intervention.
No weight-edit abliteration result reporting refusal behavior in released models.
No test of whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study analyzes directions in injected-concept detection, not whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decisions.
No test of refusal-direction transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The study compares training stages for introspective detection, not whether refusal training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
No reasoning-model evaluation of the refusal-direction claim.
